extracted.intended_audience: organizational leaders, managers, and teams responsible for crisis decision-making and communication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for leaders and teams on communicating and deciding under high-pressure, high-stakes crisis conditions (e.g., operational disasters, sudden external shocks). Emphasizes dialogue structure, psychological safety, data use, incentives, and system design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: “The structure of dialogue matters and you can make your point by making the data you’re relying on clear and inquiring of the other person, how they see it and do they see it differently from you?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When communicating under pressure, present the data you rely on, ask others how they interpret it, and invite alternative views. Use explicit data points rather than insinuation. Example: instead of joking or being sarcastic, state the specific data and ask, 'How do you see this?' Anti-pattern: using euphemisms, sarcasm, or indirect hints when stakes are high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make concerns explicit and constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have either data or concern, think of a way to air it constructively rather than avoid conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train people to say clearly, 'I am really concerned that this course/plan will cause X; I recommend Y,' rather than talking about concerns only among peers. Avoid passive references and rhetorical joking; be candid about the risk and propose a concrete alternative or course of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Teams must be psychologically safe so subordinates can raise concerns to superiors (Amy Edmondson’s concept). The El Faro bridge was not a psychologically safe space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders should cultivate norms that permit frank dissent, solicit dissenting views, and avoid reprisals. Measure and improve psychological safety through training, debriefs, and role modeling (e.g., asking for contradictory opinions). Anti-pattern: hierarchical cultures where subordinates avoid correcting superiors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit diverse perspectives and disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective leaders actively solicit opinions from different points of view and from diverse actors rather than assuming unanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During crisis discussions, explicitly ask for alternative scenarios, contradictory data interpretations, and worst-case views. Use structured prompts (e.g., 'What could go wrong? Who disagrees?') and ensure those voices are heard rather than relegated to private side conversations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid perverse incentives that compromise safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational incentives (e.g., measuring on-time arrival and factoring it into performance reviews) can pressure decision-makers to prioritize schedule over safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design performance metrics so safety-critical trade-offs are not penalized; create exceptions or explicit authority to delay/pause operations without punishment. Example: TOTE’s on-time scoring (zero if >2 hours late) created pressure to cut corners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear assignment of authority and responsibility (avoid social loafing)
rubrics_metrics.description: When many actors are responsible, individuals are less likely to assert authority (social loafing). Clear decision ownership prevents diffusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and communicate who is the ultimate decision-maker in the situation and when responsibility should be escalated. Use explicit escalation protocols and single-point accountability for critical choices. Anti-pattern: relying on implicit shared responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalate and involve shore/central management when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: If a field leader is worried, they should contact higher-ups; higher-ups can authorize safer options (e.g., longer route) when presented with concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach field leaders to escalate with clear statements of concern and proposed options. Central managers should respond permissively (e.g., 'If you’re worried, do it—safety over schedule'). Anti-pattern: leadership assuming field actors will manage risks without explicit outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of over-reliance on decision-support technology; ensure usability and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-reliance on technology combined with inadequate training can create false confidence; in the El Faro case, BVS was underused and user-unfriendly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate that users know how to operate tools and that tools surface critical scenarios accessibly. Provide regular training, simple interfaces for urgent scenarios, and checks that systems were actually consulted. Anti-pattern: assuming licenses/subscriptions equal effective use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for data latency and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Data sources can be significantly delayed or ambiguous (e.g., National Hurricane Center reports lagged ~15–18 hours; vendor analyses added hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In decision-making, explicitly account for time lags and uncertainty margins; prefer conservative buffers when data is stale or ambiguous. Use multiple data streams but account for their update cadence. Anti-pattern: treating late/aggregated outputs as real-time truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer safety margins when ambiguity exists
rubrics_metrics.description: When data is ambiguous or unusual (e.g., unexpected storm behavior), err on the side of safety rather than cutting risk margins to save cost/time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If forecasts or models are uncertain, choose routes/approaches that build slack (extra time, distance, resources). Document rationale to counterperverse incentives. Example: choosing a longer safe route rather than risking a shortcut close to a storm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design systems with slack and reduce tight coupling
rubrics_metrics.description: Perrow’s model: catastrophic failures occur when complex systems are tightly coupled. Tight coupling (no slack) magnifies perturbations into catastrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce buffers, redundancies, and decoupling where feasible (scheduling slack, spare capacity, backups) to reduce cascade risk. Recognize that efficiency gains that increase coupling raise systemic vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and review real communications (use transcripts/case studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbatim transcripts/tape recordings provide a unique opportunity to study exactly what people said and learn from communication failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reenactments, debriefs, and transcript analysis to surface communication breakdowns, norms that inhibit speaking up, and to teach improved phrasing and protocols. Incorporate case-study learning into leader training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about roles and procedures in high-risk tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear role definitions (e.g., captain, chief mate, navigation officer, officer of the deck) and cargo/procedure responsibilities reduce ambiguity under stress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure everyone understands primary duties, decision authorities in shifts, and handover procedures. Train for failure modes (who acts if engines lose power, who authorizes course changes) and confirm competency before critical operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize behavioral and cultural barriers to speaking up
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural factors (status consciousness, interpersonal friction, recent chastening events) can make subordinates avoid directly challenging leaders even when they believe a decision is dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address interpersonal dynamics proactively (team-building, rotation, mentoring), normalize dissent, and create low-cost ways to surface objections (anonymous alerts, structured questioning). Anticipate that new or chastened individuals may be less likely to speak up and compensate with explicit solicitation.
